title: Chapter 71 – Mo Lian's Scale
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The numbers do not agree, and Jian has stopped hoping they will.

He sits on the edge of his cot in Reed Courtyard at the hour before the gong, with a strip of bamboo bark on his knee and a sliver of charcoal in his fingers. Seven boys breathe around him. Ma Bao snores like a saw. Somewhere in the dark, Pei mutters a name in his sleep. Jian does not look at either of them. He looks at the bark.

It is his own ledger. He started it on the first night, because a person who owns nothing must at least own his sums. Down the left edge, in tiny cramped marks that mean nothing to anyone else, run the days. Down the right, what he has done in them.

Day 3: Terrace Nine, moonroot, ten jin cut and carried. Day 4: courtyard sweep, one point. Day 5: Terrace Nine, moonroot, ten jin. Day 6: Medicine Valley gate, hauling, half day.

Terrace Nine pays by weight. One point for every ten jin of moonroot, weighed and stamped at the Contribution Hall. He has hauled ten days' worth. He has counted each basket twice at the cutting bench, because Overseer Han, whom he has seen only twice, is a man who runs his terrace by the abacus and does not like to be corrected.

By the bark, Jian has earned eleven points on the terrace. By the duty roster, one point each day, he has earned another twelve. Twenty-three. He has spent nine on meals. He took thirty on credit at the Register.

He should be owed fourteen. He is, according to the board in the Contribution Hall, owed four.

Ten points.

He turns the charcoal over. The first time, he thought he had mis-added. The second time, he thought the Hall had docked him for something he did not know about; the Sect is made of rules nobody tells you, and the cost of learning them is usually a number. The third time, yesterday, he went through every entry in order and found that there was no single large theft.

There was a small one, every day.

Each basket of moonroot he carried to the Hall had come up a little light.

* * *

The Contribution Hall sits at the foot of the Hundred Stairs, a low wide building of gray stone with a roof of black tile and a counter forty paces long. Disciples queue along it from the first bell, outer boys in gray, servants in brown, a few inner disciples in white who do not queue but walk in at the side door and are served first. Behind the counter, clerks in blue tunics call numbers. At the far end stands a tall table with a brass scale on it, the size of a washtub, with a black iron beam and two pans on chains.

Everything passes over that scale. Herbs, ore, pelts, bones. Whatever a disciple brings in, a clerk heaves into the left pan and sets weights in the right, and the Deacon of the Hall, who stands behind the table with his hands folded and his eyes lowered, says the figure aloud and a clerk writes it.

Deacon Mo Lian says the figure aloud now.

"Nine jin and two liang."

The clerk writes it. The boy ahead of Jian, a servant with a split lip, takes his stamped slip and goes away without a word.

Jian puts his basket on the floor beside the table. He has carried it up two flights of stone from the terrace, ten jin of moonroot, rinsed and bundled, each root the length of a hand. He cut them himself. He weighed them himself, at dawn, on the small balance in the Pill Hall yard that Steward Gu lets him use because the Hall's standing order lets any Level 1 learner use it. He knows what is in the basket.

A clerk lifts it. The pan sinks. The beam swings.

"Nine jin and four liang," says Mo Lian.

His voice is soft, dry, without color. He is a man of perhaps fifty, with a long yellowed face and fine gray hair combed flat, and his hands are folded over his belt in a way Jian has already learned to dislike: too still. He has never once looked up while the scale was moving.

"I brought ten," says Jian.

The clerk's pen stops.

Mo Lian raises his eyes. It is a slow lift, a courtesy, as to a man who has asked a reasonable question. "Outer Sect Disciple?"

"Lin Jian. Reed Courtyard, number six."

"Moonroot loses moisture on the stair, Disciple. Every one who carries it knows. The Hall weighs what arrives." He inclines his head very slightly. "Nine jin four liang. The register is the register."

The register is the register.

It is not an argument. Jian knows that. It is a wall, politely built, and the whole line behind him is listening. A servant coughs. Somewhere along the counter a clerk drops a weight and swears under his breath.

"Thank you, Deacon," says Jian.

He takes his slip. He goes out into the white morning, down the steps, and stands in the cold shadow of the Hall's east wall with the slip in his hand, and does the arithmetic once more, to be sure.

Six liang. Every day. Not a single basket carried the full ten. It is too regular to be moisture.

It is the scale.

* * *

He does not scan it that day.

He wants to. There are forty-two points of cultivation energy in the Interface, and a Scan Structure on a brass beam would take a breath to run. But the Hall is full of people, and Jian's Veil is a thin thing, a slow wheel that hides what he is and not what he does. A boy who stares at a scale a little too long is a boy somebody remembers.

So he does the other thing. He goes to Steward Gu.

The steward of the Pill Hall is a short, bald, energetic man with burn scars to the elbow and a habit of speaking to his own hands. He is in the yard behind the Hall, weighing dried bark on the small balance, and he does not look up when Jian comes through the gate.

"The standing order says you may use it for learner work," says Gu, to the bark. "Not for private calculation."

"It is learner work, Steward. I need to know if my balance and yours agree."

"They agree. They are the same balance."

"No, Steward. I mean the Hall's." Jian sets down a bundle of moonroot. "If I weigh this here, and then weigh it on the Contribution Hall's scale, and the figures are different by a fixed fraction every time, what would you say is the cause?"

Gu's hands stop.

For a moment he says nothing. He turns, finally, and looks at Jian with eyes that are small and bright and very sharp, and Jian sees him see it: the boy, the bundle, the question, and the name of the man who runs that scale.

"I would say," says Gu slowly, "that the Contribution Hall's scale is a very old scale, and that it has not been reset since the autumn."

"Who resets it?"

"The Deacon." A pause. "The Deacon has been very busy, this year."

It is the most a steward can say, and Jian bows for it.

He weighs the bundle. Ten jin and a fraction, a shade heavy because the root is wet. He writes the figure on his bark, with the date, and Gu, without being asked, makes a small mark on the corner of the bark with the end of his own brush and says, to the air, "A witness may mark a figure, if the witness is a member of the Hall that owns the balance. I am a member."

"Thank you, Steward."

"I have not done anything." The steward goes back to his bark. "Do not ask me to."

* * *

It is not enough. Jian knows that, walking back through the gray afternoon. A steward's mark on a bark strip is a rumor with ink on it. The Contribution Hall will say that moonroot dries, that the Pill Hall balance is private and old, that a boy with a grievance has found a clerk who is kind to him. What he needs is something that no one can call a rumor.

He needs the register.

The register is the great book on the Contribution Hall's long table, a ledger as wide as a door, bound in black cloth and chained to a post. Every point earned or spent by every disciple of the Outer Court is written in it, in the hand of whoever handled the transaction. It cannot be taken away. It can be read, on request, by the disciple whose account it is, in the presence of a clerk, for the space of a hundred breaths.

Jian requests it on the third day after the first weighing.

He stands at the table with a clerk at his elbow, a young man with ink on his cuffs and an expression of faintly harried goodwill, and turns the heavy pages to his own number. Outer Sect 0417. His entries run down the page in a dozen different hands. Terrace Nine, moonroot, nine jin four liang. Courtyard sweep. Meal, bowl of millet. Meal.

He reads without moving his lips. He does not need a hundred breaths. He needs perhaps thirty.

The entries match his slips. The weights match what Mo Lian said aloud. Nothing is out of place.

Except the page.

It is a small thing, and he would not have seen it a month ago. But the Interface has changed how he looks at paper. He is looking not at the words but at the way the ink sits on the fiber, and the ink on the first entries, the courtyard sweep, the Register fee, the thirty points on credit, is a soft, matte, brownish black that has sunk into the page. The ink on the moonroot entries is fresher and harder, faintly glossy, and it smells, at this distance, faintly of iron.

Someone has written these twice.

He lifts his eyes to the clerk, who is looking at the ceiling with the fixed courtesy of a man pretending not to count.

"Is it permitted to copy my own account, Senior Brother?"

"On request."

"Then I request it."

It takes the clerk some time to find a clean slip. In that time, Jian stands very still with one palm flat on the cloth of the register and the other at his side, and a thin cold line of text unrolls in the corner of his eye.

```
SCAN STRUCTURE (forensic) — page fiber and ink
Cost: 5 CE
CE: 42 -> 37
Result: 11 entries overwritten within the last 20 days. Original ink: carbon-pine, aged. Overlay: carbon-iron, fresh, applied by a different hand.
Overwritten values differ from originals by +0.6 liang to -0.6 liang per entry (originals: 10 jin 0 liang).
Note: originals partially recoverable from page indentation.
```

Eleven. One for every basket of moonroot he carried to that scale. The original entry said ten jin. Someone has lifted the old ink, or painted over it, and written nine jin four liang on top.

It is not only the scale. The book is rewritten after the fact.

He copies his account onto the slip in his small cramped hand, thanks the clerk, and walks out of the Hall with his face blank and his pulse perfectly even.

It is only on the steps, in the open air, that he lets himself think the word.

Skimming.

The Deacon of the Contribution Hall is taking a sliver from every basket, and rewriting the book to cover it. Perhaps from Jian alone. Perhaps from every outer disciple. Perhaps, he thinks, climbing slowly toward the courtyard, from the whole Court.

And he cannot prove any of it. The Interface's reading is a panel in his own head. The copy on the slip will say nine jin four liang, in the Deacon's own hand.

I can prove nothing with what I have seen. I can prove it with what I can make.

* * *

He lies awake until the gong, working it out.

A Deacon who skims is a man with a fear and a purse. The purse is the points. The fear is the audit. Cheng Yun's rank has been suspended, but the Hall of Enforcement still keeps a book of its own, and Elder Duan is not a man who looks kindly on a clerk who cooks accounts. Mo Lian knows that. He has rigged his scale very carefully, a sliver at a time, small enough that no single disciple will risk a complaint, regular enough to pay for itself over a season.

The only way to beat a man like that is to make him prefer to stop.

And the only way to make him prefer to stop is to put something in front of him that is worth more than the sliver.

Points.

The Sect pays in points for four things: labor, herbs, pills and ideas. Labor is what the Deacon has been skimming. Herbs go over his scale. Pills pass through the Pill Hall, and Jian holds a learner's leave there, with a Level 1 furnace he is allowed to light twice a week, and no Elder to speak for him.

That leaves ideas.

Every Hall in the Sect keeps a roll of recipes and methods and tricks of the trade, and every Hall will, under the old rule of the Founders, pay for an improvement. It is a small, dull rule, hidden in the back pages of the Sect Handbook that nobody reads. A disciple who submits a method, formula or device that shortens a craft, saves a reagent or raises a yield, and whose submission is confirmed by two trials, shall be paid in points from the Hall's account, according to the saving.

Jian found it on his third night, reading by the one candle Ma Bao has agreed not to notice.

He has a method.

* * *

The public Breath-Gathering pill is the first thing any outer disciple learns to make. It is a Level 1 pill of the low tier, dull, cheap, and reliable. It takes four herbs: moonroot, red bark, dew-lily and a pinch of stone-salt. Every furnace in the Outer Court makes it. Every apprentice burns a batch before he gets one right.

The public recipe grinds the herbs together. All four, at once, in the stone mortar, and then adds them to the furnace.

Jian tried that on his first day. He got a gray muddy paste, and a pill that cracked.

He thought: The salt eats the bark.

He knows it because he had the Interface scan the failed batch, and the panel told him, in its patient flat way, that the stone-salt had bound with the red bark's resin during grinding and locked a fifth of its potency into an inert crust. It is the sort of thing that a hundred years of apprentices must have noticed and shrugged at, because the pill came out good enough.

On his second batch he ground the moonroot and the lily first, added the bark second, and folded the salt in at the very end, off the heat. The pill came out glossy, evenly colored, with a faint ring of green at the edge that the Steward called, with a grudging eyebrow, unusual.

It tested at one-sixth stronger than the public pill. Same herbs. Same weight. Same cost.

He writes it that night on a clean strip, in his plainest hand, as a method and not a secret. A change in the order of grinding. Salt last, off the heat. Result: pill potency raised by one-sixth, herbs unchanged. He signs it Outer Sect 0417. He adds nothing about the Interface and nothing about scans.

In the morning he takes it to Steward Gu.

"A method," says Gu, to his hands.

"Under the Founders' Rule, Steward."

"I know the rule." The steward turns the strip over once, twice. His small bright eyes go from the page to Jian and back. "It requires two trials."

"I would like Elder Bai to witness one."

Gu laughs. It is a short surprised bark. "You would like the Elder of the Pill Hall to stand in a yard at dawn and watch a boy grind bark."

"Yes, Steward."

For a moment the steward looks as though he is going to refuse. Then something changes in the line of his shoulders, and he says, "He is in the furnace room. He does not like to be disturbed." He puts the strip into his sleeve. "Come back at noon."

* * *

Elder Bai does not look like a Foundation alchemist.

Jian has met him only once, on the second day, and the impression is the same now: a stout, genial, rumpled man, with a belly and a round pink face and the sleeves of his robe pushed to the elbow and stained to the wrist with something green. There is a plum stone in the corner of his mouth. He is, as far as Jian can tell, always eating.

He takes the bark in his left hand and the pestle in his right and says, "Show me," and sits down on a stool in the yard to watch.

Jian shows him.

He does it twice, plainly, the old way and the new. The mortar is stone, the furnace is a clay thing the size of a kettle, and the herbs are weighed on the small balance, with Gu watching and the Elder chewing. It takes most of an hour. At the end Bai takes up one pill of each, bites each cleanly in half, rolls the halves around his mouth for an uncomfortably long moment, and spits both into the dirt.

"Hm," he says.

Nobody speaks.

"One-sixth," says Bai. "It is a little more than one-sixth. I would say one-fifth, with a better furnace." He looks at Jian. His eyes are small and pale and extraordinarily direct. "Who told you to put the salt last?"

"No one, Elder. The first batch cracked."

"Did it."

"It cracked at the edge. As if something had hardened."

"And so you moved the salt." The Elder rubs his chin. "A hundred and thirty years this Hall has made Breath-Gathering. I made it myself for sixty of them. I have burned a thousand batches that cracked at the edge." He is not smiling. "Do you know what I did when they cracked?"

"No, Elder."

"I added more bark." A short dry chuckle. "It did not occur to me that the salt was the matter. It did not occur to anyone." He leans back. "You are a very careless sort of boy, Lin Jian, to give this away."

"It is for the points, Elder."

"I know what it is for." The pale eyes flick, very briefly, toward the gate, toward the long gray roof of the Contribution Hall visible above the wall. "I am an old man, not a stupid one. Gu has told me about your moonroot."

Jian says nothing. It is the safest thing. In his head, a small cold voice remarks: Gu has told him. The steward who 'has not done anything.'

"I will confirm your method," says Bai. "Two trials. Gu will witness the second." He stands, with a grunt, and dusts his hands on his robe. "Eighty points."

Eighty.

It is more than three weeks of Terrace Nine. It is more, he realizes, than he expected by a factor of two.

"It will be entered in the Pill Hall's register, not the Contribution Hall's," says Bai. "In my hand. With my seal." The pale eyes rest on him. "I do not suppose you object."

"No, Elder."

"I thought not." He puts the plum stone into the dirt. "And the method becomes the Hall's. Any apprentice may use it. You have no claim on it, no right of first use. You understand?"

The cost.

Jian had priced it already, in the dark, before he wrote the strip. A method sold is a method shared. Every outer disciple who makes the pill will make it better, and the Pill Hall's output will rise by a fifth, and in a season the thing that makes Jian's batches unusual will be the thing that makes every batch ordinary. What he sells for eighty points is the right to be the only boy in the Outer Court who knows.

"I understand, Elder."

"Then we are agreed." Bai turns, mid-stride, with the rumpled unhurried gait of a man walking to his lunch. "You will wish to deposit it yourself. The Contribution Hall prefers to see its customers."

* * *

The Contribution Hall prefers nothing of the kind.

The Deacon is at his table when Jian arrives, hands folded, eyes down. A clerk takes the Pill Hall's chit, a thin red slip stamped with Bai's plum-colored seal, and carries it to the register. The great black book is opened. A brush is dipped.

Eighty points. Method: Breath-Gathering. Paid by the Pill Hall.

The clerk writes it. Jian watches the ink go down. It is the soft matte brown of the old register, carbon-pine, because it is the clerk's own ink, from the Hall's own bottle. He does not move.

"Eighty," says Mo Lian, softly. "A generous valuation for a first method."

"The Elder was kind."

"The Elder is always kind." The Deacon's eyes are lowered. "I notice that you are also a person who counts."

It is said quite gently. There is nothing in it, no threat, no warning. It is a remark.

"I count what I carry, Deacon."

"I have heard so." A pause. "I have heard that you carried ten jin of moonroot, nine days out of ten, and were weighed at nine jin four liang."

The Hall is very full. There are at least thirty people within earshot. Jian says, in a clear voice that carries just as far:

"Yes, Deacon. Nine jin four liang. I am obliged to you for the figure."

Someone in the queue coughs. A clerk, farther down the table, has stopped writing.

Mo Lian looks up.

It is the first time Jian has seen the whole of his face. It is the face of a man who has spent thirty years in a room, with the pallor and the stoop and the careful flat patience of a person who has never been seen to hurry. But the eyes, he thinks, are wrong. They are too steady. They do not move as eyes do when a man is working out a sum.

They move like a pair of lamps on a wall.

"Disciple Lin," says the Deacon. "Come to my office at the sixth bell. We will settle your account."

* * *

The Deacon's office is a narrow room behind the Hall, with a desk and a lamp and a single window with a bar across it. There are books on the wall. There is a stool for visitors. There is no tea.

Jian comes alone at the sixth bell, in his gray tunic, with his bark ledger in his sleeve and his copy of the register slip folded in his cuff. He has told no one. He has told Pebble, who is asleep in the bag at his belt and will remain so for another twelve days, and who does not answer.

Mo Lian is behind the desk with his hands folded.

"Sit."

"Thank you, Deacon. I prefer to stand."

"As you like." The Deacon's voice is exactly as soft as it was in the Hall. "You have a complaint."

"No, Deacon. I have a sum."

"A sum."

Jian takes out the bark. He lays it on the desk, not close, the width of a hand from the Deacon's folded fingers. He does not speak until the Deacon's eyes have moved to it.

"Eleven baskets of moonroot. Each weighed at dawn on the Pill Hall's balance before carrying: ten jin, and a fraction. Each weighed at the Contribution Hall's scale: nine jin four liang. The fraction is constant. The Pill Hall's steward has witnessed three of the weighings and marked them." He keeps his voice level. "Eleven entries in my account in the register. All written, I believe, in the same week."

"The register is..."

"The register is the register. Yes." He takes out the slip, unfolds it, lays it beside the bark. "I copied my account with a clerk's leave. The first entries are in carbon-pine ink. The moonroot entries are in a different ink. It has a different gloss." He does not say and a different smell. He does not say forensic scan. He says, steadily, "I am a first-year, Deacon. I do not know what the rules say about a clerk who writes a page twice. But I know what the Founders' Rule says about a man who adjusts a weight."

The Deacon does not move.

"It says," says Jian, "that the adjusting of a weight in the Hall's favor, by any officer, is a theft from the whole Court, and shall be answered to the Hall of Enforcement." He lets that sit. "I have not taken it to Elder Duan. I have a Level 1 furnace and eighty points and a month of work. I do not want a war. I want my ten jin."

It is very quiet.

The lamp ticks. Somewhere in the Hall a bell strikes the quarter. Mo Lian's long yellowed face has not changed by a line. But his hands, the folded hands, have begun, very slightly, to turn: the right thumb pressing the left knuckle, once, twice, like a man testing a lock.

"You are ten," says the Deacon at last.

"Yes, Deacon."

"A youth of twenty does not carry a ledger. A youth of twenty does not write in the Founders' Rule. Who taught you?"

"My mother," says Jian, "taught me to count."

It is true. It is the truest lie he has ever told. Su Qinghe taught him sums at the kitchen table in Green Pine Hill, with beans.

Mo Lian looks at him for a long time.

"The scale," he says finally, "is old. It drifts. I shall have it reset." His voice has not altered. "I shall also have the register corrected. If there has been an error in your account, I will see that it is made good. Ten points, I think. In addition to your eighty."

It is a bribe. It is also a surrender. Jian bows, exactly as far as a first-year should bow to a Deacon, and not an inch further.

"Thank you, Deacon."

"You may go."

He goes. He keeps his back straight, down the corridor, through the gate, across the courtyard, and into the white blaze of the afternoon. He does not look back. He is nearly to the stairs before he lets himself breathe.

It worked.

He has not been so afraid since the ford.

* * *

The thing he notices, he notices late.

He is at the foot of the Hundred Stairs, in the shadow of the first landing, watching a line of inner disciples in white come down in pairs from the upper terraces. A gong sounds. The afternoon light is long and clear and falls, as he turns back toward the Contribution Hall, on the office window, a bar-crossed square of glass on the second floor.

Mo Lian is standing at it.

He has not moved from the desk, Jian thinks. He would not have heard the door. He is standing very still, with his back half turned, with one hand raised against the glass in the loose slack way of a man leaning on a wall. The light is behind him. Jian sees the shape of the hand, long, yellowed, flat against the pane.

He sees that it is shaking.

It is not a tremor of age. It is not fear. He has seen fear in hands; he saw it in Hu's, in the forge, before the tremor was cured. This is something finer and stranger: a rapid, rhythmic quiver, like a taut thread, as if the hand were a glass struck by a distant note.

And on the pane, where the fingertips rest, there is a mark.

It is a thin dark smear, no longer than a grain of rice, where something has bled from the pad of the thumb onto the glass. It is not red. It is the brown-black of old iron, glossy and hard, and even from forty paces, even through a pane of glass and the long amber light, Jian knows what it is.

The same ink.

The same ink that lies, fresh and harder, on the moonroot pages of the register. The same iron smell. The same faint rust under the thumbnail he saw in the Hall on the day of the Register.

It is not ink at all.

Mo Lian does not turn. He lifts the hand from the glass, slowly, and looks at it, and then, with the unhurried air of a man pocketing a coin, wipes the thumb on the hem of his sleeve.

Then he looks down, directly, through the window, at Jian.

And smiles.
